newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition inches towards budget deal.
newsitem.headline: German coalition inches towards budget deal.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government on Wednesday pressed on with the painstaking work of drafting a 1997 budget after agreeing to put on ice a damaging row over cutting an unpopular tax to rebuild eastern Germany.

That, however, was about all the three-party alliance agreed to at two sessions of talks on Tuesday, keeping Finance Minister Theo Waigel under intense pressure to conjure a budget which will make Germany fit for European monetary union.

Waigel, defending his record against attacks from both within and outside the government, said his ninth budget would meet the Maastricht treaty's strict targets even though there has been a big overshoot in borrowing this year.
"We will be within plan in 1997," he told Stern magazine in an interview to be published on Thursday.

Kohl called in ministers from his Christian Democrat (CDU) party to hunt for more savings after a row which has taken his 14-year-old coalition with the Christian Social Union (CSU) and the liberal Free Democrats close to collapse.
The FDP has blocked tax increases to cover mounting gaps in next year's budget plans which could open further if tax revenue estimates due out on Friday show a further shortfall.
"The tail is wagging the dog. The FDP is succeeding in forcing the CDU/CSU into the most absurd contortions -- and the Chancellor lets it happen," the Sueddeutsche Zeiting commented.
Waigel has committed himself to hitting the Maastricht treaty's debt and budget deficit limits of 60 percent and three percent of gross domestic product respectively next year.
Those goals underpin Germany's demand for a tough stability pact to enforce budget discipline on countries wanting to join the planned launch of the single European currency in 1999.
Despite warnings from Brussels that the pact would be delayed into next year, the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday it was confident agreement could be reached.

After Tuesday's meeting, Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said talks on cutting the "solidarity tax" -- a 7.5 percent surcharge on taxes owed -- would be put back until mid-December. The FDP wants a two-point cut in 1998, a demand that Kohl and Waigel are not yet ready to accept.
Waigel is also expected to hold further talks with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) -- who can block tax measures in parliament's upper house -- over reforming corporate taxes.
Meanwhile, the coalition will concentrate on readying its budget by early next week for passage through parliament at the end of November.
FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle, trying to patch up strained coalition relations, said the tax row had been "a storm which has cleared the air."
"I expect that there will be no problems in passing the budget," Westerwelle told ZDF television.
And, although Waigel hinted in the Stern interview that he may be ready to quit the finance portfolio and take over as foreign minister, that move is regarded as unlikely.
The only alternative to the status quo, the Sueddeutsche Zeitung noted, would be for Kohl to extend his record run as Chancellor at the head of a grand coalition with the SPD.
That is something none of the three ruling parties want.
